articles.title: For the first time, the Australian government has exercised its powers to cancel an entire course
articles.summary: In late 2025, the Australian Parliament passed legislative amendments expanding government oversight and regulatory powers over the international education sector, including through updates to the National Code of Practice for Providers of Education and Training to Overseas Students. This marked the first time the Australian government used its newly granted authority to cancel an entire course.
articles.insight:
This development signals growing regulatory scrutiny of course quality and compliance in Australia’s international education sector, potentially influencing student perceptions of institutional stability—though direct impacts on global demand remain uncertain without evidence of broader enforcement trends or spillover to other English-speaking destinations.  
Admissions teams should monitor Australian government announcements on course cancellations, student visa refusal rates, and source-market sentiment surveys—particularly in key regions like India and China—to assess whether regulatory tightening begins affecting application volumes or institutional reputation relative to peer destinations.

articles.title: Canada increases proof of funds requirement
articles.summary: Canada has raised the proof of funds requirement for study permit applicants to reflect current cost-of-living conditions. This change was reported by The PIE News.
articles.insight:
Canada’s higher proof of funds requirement may modestly dampen application volumes from cost-sensitive markets, particularly where students rely on family savings or informal lending, though broader demand trends depend on concurrent factors like exchange rates and program quality.  
Admissions teams should track application data from Canadian competitor institutions and monitor social media sentiment in key source countries—especially India, Nigeria, and the Philippines—to detect early shifts in student preference or perceived affordability.

articles.title: August applications for UK study visas fall 16% in just a year
articles.summary: New UK government figures show that study visa applications submitted after August fell by 16% year-on-year. This decline has raised concerns about the decreasing number of international students applying to study in the UK.
articles.insight:
The 16% year-on-year drop in UK study visa applications post-August may reflect tightening visa policies, rising costs, or shifting perceptions—though it’s unclear whether this signals broader demand erosion or short-term policy adjustment affecting specific cohorts.  
Admissions teams should track application trends by region and level, compare UK competitor destinations’ visa data, and assess whether messaging around affordability, post-study work rights, or regulatory clarity needs refinement ahead of peak recruitment cycles.

articles.title: CAS issuances down 27% as UK visa refusals jump 30%, Enroly data shows
articles.summary: Enroly’s data shows that Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS) issuances have decreased by 27% while UK visa refusals have increased by 30%. South Asian and African countries have been the most affected by these changes amid the UK’s heightened compliance requirements.
articles.insight:
The 27% drop in UK CAS issuances alongside a 30% rise in visa refusals—especially for South Asian and African applicants—suggests tightening UK compliance may be dampening application conversion, though it remains unclear whether this reflects reduced demand, stricter scrutiny, or procedural delays.  
Admissions teams should monitor real-time application volumes and refusal reasons from key source countries, while reviewing their pre-application support and documentation guidance to ensure alignment with evolving UKVI expectations and student preparedness.

articles.title: Foreign, mainland students flock to Hong Kong, sparking property demand in education sector
articles.summary: Hong Kong is projected to host around 200,000 non-local students by 2035 as part of its push to become a global education hub, according to CBRE. To accommodate an estimated 30,000 to 40,000 non-local students in international schools, 40 to 50 new campuses will be needed, requiring up to an additional 1.11 million square metres of real estate.
articles.insight:
Hong Kong’s ambitious expansion of international school capacity signals growing regional competition for mainland Chinese students, though its direct impact on tertiary recruitment in the US, UK, Australia, and NZ remains uncertain amid shifting visa policies and family preferences for degree-level destinations.  
Admissions teams should monitor enrolment trends in Hong Kong’s new international schools and associated parental migration patterns, as early education choices may foreshadow longer-term higher education decision-making—particularly among high-income, mobile mainland families.

articles.title: US government warns universities to limit their authorisation of Curricular Practical Training work placements
articles.summary: The U.S. government, under the Trump administration, has issued warnings to universities urging them to limit their authorizations of Curricular Practical Training (CPT) work placements for international students. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) stated in internal memos that the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) has observed an increase in CPT authorizations that fail to meet regulatory requirements.
articles.insight:
This development signals potential tightening of U.S. post-study work flexibility for international students, which may dampen U.S. appeal—especially among students from India and China prioritising CPT as a pathway to employment, though broader demand trends remain influenced by multiple factors including tuition, safety, and alternative destinations.  
Admissions teams should track CPT policy updates closely, assess how peer institutions are adjusting advising and programme structures, and begin reviewing whether their curricula align with evolving regulatory expectations—particularly for STEM and business programmes heavily reliant on CPT placements.
